summary:
FireChronicle is an India focused satellite fire intelligence platform designed to harmonize NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active fire observations into a more consistent and understandable picture of fire activity across geographical regions and time.

Different satellite sensors observe thermal anomalies at different spatial resolutions and with different detection characteristics, making their raw hotspot records difficult to compare directly. FireChronicle addresses this challenge through a unified geospatial data workflow that standardizes satellite observations, compares detections using spatial and temporal correspondence, and organizes observed activity into an interactive geographical map and historical burning activity calendar.

The platform is designed to help users explore hotspot locations, inspect satellite brightness temperature and Fire Radiative Power (FRP), compare MODIS and VIIRS observations, examine unmatched detections, and investigate historical patterns.

With an India first approach, FireChronicle also incorporates relevant Indian geospatial and forest/agricultural-fire information where accessible, providing additional context for interpreting satellite observations.

By preserving original sensor measurements, documenting harmonization methods, and making data provenance and uncertainty visible, FireChronicle aims to make satellite fire information more comparable and useful for researchers, environmental analysts and fire-management stakeholders.
details:
The problem

Satellites have monitored active-fire hotspots for decades, but the record is distributed across instruments with different spatial resolutions, spectral characteristics, observation times, detection sensitivities and confidence definitions. MODIS (Terra and Aqua) provides a long historical record at a nominal active-fire pixel scale of approximately 1 km, while the VIIRS 375 m active-fire product provides finer spatial detail and can detect some smaller fires that coarser products may not resolve.

Consequently, raw hotspot counts from MODIS and VIIRS cannot simply be added or compared as though each detection represented an equivalent observation. The same burning activity may be observed by both sensors, one sensor may detect activity the other misses, and the satellites may observe an area at different times. Without a transparent comparison method, sensor differences can be mistaken for changes in fire activity.

This limits the ability to build consistent historical activity calendars and compare burning patterns across sensors and years.

Our solution

FireChronicle is a geospatial web application designed to make MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations easier to compare and interpret. It preserves the source records and their original measurements, transforms them into a common analytical structure, identifies plausible cross-sensor correspondences using spatial and temporal criteria, and aggregates observations into a documented geographical and temporal framework.

The application is designed around an India-first area of interest while retaining the ability to examine other regions when appropriate data are available.

How it works

  1. Data ingestion: Import NASA FIRMS active-fire archive files and, when configured and available, retrieve observations through the documented FIRMS API.
  2. Data inspection and validation: Identify the product, collection, satellite, date coverage, geographic coverage, source fields, invalid records and missing values.
  3. Standardization: Normalize timestamps to UTC and harmonize shared field names while retaining original sensor-specific fields and product metadata.
  4. Geographic filtering: Select observations within the chosen area of interest using a documented India boundary or another user-selected boundary.
  5. Spatial and temporal comparison: Identify candidate MODIS–VIIRS correspondences using configurable distance and time criteria. Preserve unmatched detections rather than treating them as errors.
  6. Common-grid aggregation: Summarize source-specific observations by date and spatial cell using a clearly documented grid definition.
  7. Visualization and exploration: Present detections, sensor comparisons and historical activity through an interactive map, activity calendar and analytical charts.
  8. Provenance and uncertainty: Retain source identifiers, processing choices, thresholds, units and limitations so users can understand how each result was produced.

What users can explore

  • Individual MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations on a map.
  • Acquisition date and time in UTC, sensor/platform and geographical coordinates.
  • Original source-specific confidence attributes.
  • Brightness temperature in Kelvin, with the original sensor channel identified.
  • Fire Radiative Power in megawatts (MW).
  • Candidate cross-sensor correspondences, spatial distance and time difference.
  • Sensor-specific and unmatched observations.
  • Daily and monthly burning-activity summaries on a common grid.
  • Historical activity patterns and, when sufficient comparable history exists, unusual-activity indicators.
  • Data sources, processing methods, filters and uncertainty.

India-first application

FireChronicle prioritizes India as its initial geographical focus. Its intended contextual sources include Forest Survey of India forest-fire information, ISRO/NRSC Bhuvan agricultural-fire and geospatial layers, and Indian land-cover information. These sources can help users understand the geographical setting of satellite observations.

Contextual evidence must not be mistaken for ground truth. A hotspot near forest land is not automatically a confirmed forest fire, and a hotspot during a crop-burning season is not automatically a confirmed agricultural burn. The interface should label such interpretations as contextual associations or likely classifications and expose the supporting source.

Why it matters

A consistent view of satellite-observed burning activity can support historical analysis, research, monitoring and the prioritization of areas for further investigation. FireChronicle aims to reduce the effort required to compare separate satellite records and make the limitations of those comparisons visible to users.

Scientific limitations

A satellite active-fire hotspot is a thermal detection, not necessarily a unique wildfire, fire perimeter, incident report or confirmed cause. Brightness temperature is a satellite-channel measurement in Kelvin; it is not the exact temperature of a flame. FRP measures the rate of radiative energy release in MW and is not burned area. MODIS and VIIRS confidence definitions are different and should not be treated as a common calibrated probability without a validated transformation. Days without detections do not prove that no fire occurred, because observation coverage, clouds, overpass timing and detection limits matter.
